question: During a pre-trip inspection, what does rust around the wheel nuts most likely indicate?
choice_a: The nuts may be loose and tightness should be checked
choice_b: The brake drums are overheating
choice_c: The tires were recently rotated
choice_d: The wheel bearings need lubrication
explanation: Rust around wheel nuts may mean the nuts are loose, so tightness should be checked; after a tire has been changed you should stop a short while later and re-check nut tightness.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Wheel and Rim Problems

question: Which of the following wheel or rim conditions is considered dangerous during a vehicle inspection?
choice_a: A tire with a new valve stem cap
choice_b: A wheel that was recently balanced
choice_c: A wheel or rim that has had a welding repair
choice_d: A wheel with a factory paint coating
explanation: The manual states that wheels or rims that have had welding repairs are not safe.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Wheel and Rim Problems

question: In a multi-leaf spring, what proportion of missing leaves will put the vehicle 'out of service'?
choice_a: Any single leaf missing
choice_b: One-half or more
choice_c: One-fourth or more
choice_d: Three-fourths or more
explanation: The manual states that if one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing from a leaf spring, the vehicle will be put 'out of service,' though any defect could be dangerous.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Suspension System Defects

question: Why are broken or cracked spring hangers considered extremely dangerous?
choice_a: They cause the engine to overheat
choice_b: They reduce fuel efficiency
choice_c: They can allow the axle to move out of its proper position
choice_d: They make the steering wheel loose
explanation: The suspension system holds up the vehicle and its load and keeps the axles in place; cracked or broken spring hangers can allow movement of the axle from its proper position.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Suspension System Defects

question: Which of the following is a defect to look for when inspecting brake drums or shoes?
choice_a: Shoes that are painted black
choice_b: Shoes or pads with oil, grease, or brake fluid on them
choice_c: Drums that are slightly warm to the touch
choice_d: Shoes with a manufacturer stamp
explanation: The manual lists shoes or pads contaminated with oil, grease, or brake fluid, along with cracked drums and dangerously thin, missing, or broken shoes, as brake defects to check for.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Bad Brake Drums or Shoes

question: On a 20-inch steering wheel, how much play at the rim corresponds to the maximum steering wheel free play of 10 degrees before steering becomes difficult?
choice_a: Approximately 12 inches
choice_b: Approximately 6 inches
choice_c: Approximately 2 inches
choice_d: Approximately 1/2 inch
explanation: The manual states that steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees (approximately 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel) can make it hard to steer.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Steering System Defects

question: If a vehicle is equipped with power steering, what should be checked during inspection?
choice_a: The cruise control switch
choice_b: Hoses, pumps, and fluid level, and check for leaks
choice_c: Only the horn button
choice_d: The radio antenna mount
explanation: The manual instructs that if the vehicle is power-steering equipped, you should check hoses, pumps, and fluid level, and check for leaks.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Steering System Defects

question: Why is a broken exhaust system especially dangerous on a commercial motor vehicle?
choice_a: It can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth
choice_b: It always causes a fire immediately
choice_c: It voids the vehicle registration
choice_d: It automatically disables the brakes
explanation: The manual warns that a broken exhaust system can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Exhaust System Defects

question: According to the vehicle inspection requirements, what warning devices should a commercial vehicle carry for parking on the roadway?
choice_a: A whistle and a flag
choice_b: A single road flare only
choice_c: One reflective triangle
choice_d: Three reflective triangles, or at least 6 fuses, or 3 liquid-burning flares
explanation: The manual specifies that vehicles must carry warning devices for parked vehicles: three reflective triangles, or at least 6 fuses, or 3 liquid-burning flares.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Emergency Equipment

question: Before each trip, what must a truck driver verify about the cargo?
choice_a: That the cargo has a bar code label
choice_b: That the truck is not overloaded and the cargo is balanced and secured
choice_c: That the cargo is insured for double its value
choice_d: That the cargo weighs less than the fuel tank capacity
explanation: The manual states you must make sure the truck is not overloaded and the cargo is balanced and secured before each trip, and if it contains hazardous materials you must inspect for proper papers and placarding.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1, Cargo (Trucks)

question: What must a motor carrier do about defects noted on a vehicle inspection report?
choice_a: Discard the report after 24 hours regardless of defects
choice_b: Only repair items if the driver requests it in writing
choice_c: Repair items that affect safety and certify on the report that repairs were made or were unnecessary
choice_d: Forward the report to the vehicle manufacturer for repair
explanation: The manual states that the motor carrier must repair any items in the report that affect safety and certify on the report that repairs were made or were unnecessary.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 1: Vehicle Overview

question: Before raising the hood or tilting the cab to check the engine compartment, what should you first confirm?
choice_a: That the radio is turned off
choice_b: That the parking brakes are on and/or wheels are chocked
choice_c: That the cargo doors are open
choice_d: That the fuel tank is full
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to check that the parking brakes are on and/or wheels chocked before raising the hood or tilting the cab.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 2: Check Engine Compartment

topic: Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Cab
question: When starting the engine as part of the in-cab inspection, what should be true of the ABS indicator light on the dash?
choice_a: It should never illuminate at all
choice_b: It should come on and then turn off
choice_c: It should flash continuously while driving
choice_d: It should stay on for the entire trip
explanation: The manual states the ABS indicator light should come on and then turn off; if it stays on, the ABS is not working properly.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: For a vehicle with air brakes, how quickly should air pressure build from 50 to 90 psi according to the manual?
choice_a: Within 3 minutes
choice_b: Within 15 minutes
choice_c: Within 30 seconds
choice_d: Within 1 hour
explanation: The manual states air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: What is the typical governor cut-out air pressure range mentioned in the manual, at which the air compressor should stop pumping air?
choice_a: Usually around 10 to 20 psi
choice_b: Usually around 50 to 60 psi
choice_c: Usually around 200 to 220 psi
choice_d: Usually around 120 to 140 psi
explanation: The manual states you should build air pressure to governor cut-out, usually around 120 to 140 psi, while noting drivers should know their vehicle's specific requirements.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: At the start of the walk-around inspection, what should you check at the front of the vehicle regarding lights?
choice_a: That the license plate light works only
choice_b: That the low beams and both four-way flashers are working, then check high beams with the dimmer switch
choice_c: That the interior dome light is off
choice_d: That the fog lights are disconnected
explanation: The manual describes going to the front of the vehicle to check that low beams are on and both four-way flashers are working, then pushing the dimmer switch to check that high beams work.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 5: Do Walk-around Inspection

topic: Left Front Wheel and Tire Check
question: During the walk-around inspection of the left front wheel, how can a driver test for rust-streaked lug nuts that may indicate looseness?
choice_a: Spray them with water
choice_b: Shine a flashlight on them
choice_c: Tap them with a screwdriver handle
choice_d: Use a wrench to test them
explanation: The manual instructs to use a wrench to test rust-streaked lug nuts, which indicate looseness.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 5: Do Walk-around Inspection -- Left Front Side

question: What color should the clearance, identification, and taillights be at the rear of the vehicle?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: White
choice_c: Amber
choice_d: Blue
explanation: The manual states that rear clearance and identification lights, and taillights, should be clean, operating, and the proper color, which is red at the rear.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 5: Do Walk-around Inspection -- Rear

question: During inspection of dual tires on the right rear, what should a driver check for besides inflation and tread wear?
choice_a: That the tires were manufactured in the same week
choice_b: That the valve caps are painted red
choice_c: That both tires are the same brand of paint
choice_d: That the tires are not rubbing each other and nothing is stuck between them
explanation: The manual instructs checking that dual tires are not rubbing each other and that nothing is stuck between them, in addition to inflation, valve stems/caps, and tread wear.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 5: Do Walk-around Inspection -- Right Rear

question: When checking stop lights during Step 6 of the inspection, if you have no helper, how can you activate the stop lights while outside the vehicle?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand brake
choice_b: Rev the engine to high rpm
choice_c: Turn the steering wheel fully left
choice_d: Open the driver's door
explanation: The manual notes that to check the stop lights, you apply the trailer hand brake (or have a helper put on the brake pedal).
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 6: Check Signal Lights

question: How do you test a vehicle with hydraulic brakes for leaks during the final inspection step?
choice_a: Check only the brake fluid color
choice_b: Release the parking brake and coast downhill
choice_c: Pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold for five seconds; the pedal should not move
choice_d: Rev the engine to full throttle while braking
explanation: The manual instructs pumping the brake pedal three times, then applying firm pressure and holding for five seconds; if the pedal moves, there may be a leak or other problem.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Step 7: Start the Engine and Check

question: How should a driver test that the parking brake holds during a pre-trip inspection?
choice_a: Accelerate to highway speed and then apply the parking brake
choice_b: Place the vehicle in a low gear and gently pull forward against the set parking brake
choice_c: Turn off the engine and coast downhill
choice_d: Shift into reverse and apply full throttle
explanation: The manual describes setting the parking brake, placing the vehicle into a low gear, and gently pulling forward against the parking brake to make sure it holds.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Brake System -- Test Parking Brake(s)

question: How should a driver test the service brake's stopping action during a pre-trip inspection?
choice_a: Drive at highway speed and slam the brakes
choice_b: Apply the brakes only while parked
choice_c: Go about five miles per hour and push the brake pedal firmly, checking for pulling to one side
choice_d: Test only in reverse gear
explanation: The manual instructs going about five miles per hour, pushing the brake pedal firmly, and noting that 'pulling' to one side or unusual pedal feel can mean brake trouble.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.5, Brake System -- Test Service Brake Stopping Action

question: How often must drivers of trucks and truck tractors transporting cargo inspect the cargo's securement during a trip?
choice_a: Only once at the start of the trip
choice_b: Every 500 miles regardless of time
choice_c: Within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first
choice_d: Only when crossing state lines
explanation: The manual states drivers must inspect cargo securement within the first 50 miles of a trip and every 150 miles or every three hours (whichever comes first) after that.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.6, Inspection during a Trip

question: What is the purpose of the after-trip vehicle inspection report?
choice_a: To report anything affecting safety or possibly leading to mechanical breakdown
choice_b: To log the driver's meal breaks
choice_c: To document fuel prices at each stop
choice_d: To record the driver's personal mileage reimbursement
explanation: The manual states a driver may have to make a written report each day on the vehicle's condition, reporting anything affecting safety or possibly leading to mechanical breakdown.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.1.7, After-trip Inspection and Report

question: On a hill, what should a driver with a manual transmission vehicle do before taking their right foot off the brake to prevent rolling back?
choice_a: Partly engage the clutch
choice_b: Shift into neutral
choice_c: Fully release the clutch
choice_d: Turn off the engine
explanation: The manual instructs that with a manual transmission, you should partly engage the clutch before taking your right foot off the brake, and apply the parking brake whenever necessary to keep from rolling back.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.1, Accelerating

question: On a tractor-trailer equipped with a trailer brake hand valve, how can the driver prevent the vehicle from rolling back on a hill?
choice_a: Increase tire pressure
choice_b: Disconnect the trailer air lines
choice_c: Shift the trailer into reverse
choice_d: Apply the hand valve to hold the vehicle
explanation: The manual notes that on a tractor-trailer equipped with a trailer brake hand valve, the hand valve can be applied to keep the vehicle from rolling back.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.1, Accelerating

question: Why should a driver speed up smoothly and gradually rather than accelerating roughly?
choice_a: It is required only in school zones
choice_b: It reduces tire pressure requirements
choice_c: Rough acceleration can cause mechanical damage and, when pulling a trailer, damage the coupling
choice_d: It improves the radio reception
explanation: The manual states that speeding up smoothly and gradually prevents the vehicle from jerking, since rough acceleration can cause mechanical damage and, when pulling a trailer, can damage the coupling.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.1, Accelerating

question: What should a driver do if the drive wheels begin to spin while accelerating on a surface with poor traction, such as rain or snow?
choice_a: Apply the parking brake
choice_b: Take their foot off the accelerator
choice_c: Shift into a higher gear immediately
choice_d: Press the accelerator harder to power through
explanation: The manual advises that if the drive wheels begin to spin, you should take your foot off the accelerator, since using too much power on poor traction can cause loss of control.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.1, Accelerating

question: How should a driver hold the steering wheel to avoid losing control if a curb or pothole is struck?
choice_a: With fingertips only for quick release
choice_b: Loosely with one hand at the top
choice_c: Firmly with both hands on opposite sides of the wheel
choice_d: With both hands on the same side of the wheel
explanation: The manual instructs holding the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides, because hitting a curb or pothole could pull the wheel away from your hands without a firm hold.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.2, Steering

question: On a vehicle with a manual transmission, when should the driver push in the clutch while stopping?
choice_a: As soon as the brake pedal is first touched
choice_b: Only after the vehicle has fully stopped
choice_c: Immediately upon seeing a hazard, before braking
choice_d: When the engine is close to idle
explanation: The manual states that with a manual transmission, you should push the clutch in when the engine is close to idle while bringing the vehicle to a smooth, safe stop.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.3, Stopping

question: What general strategy does the manual recommend regarding backing a commercial vehicle?
choice_a: Back only using the passenger-side mirror
choice_b: Never use a helper, as it distracts the driver
choice_c: Always back into parking spaces at high speed to minimize exposure time
choice_d: Avoid backing whenever possible, and try to park so you can pull forward when leaving
explanation: The manual states that because you cannot see everything behind your vehicle, backing is always dangerous, so you should avoid backing when you can and try to park so you can pull forward when you leave.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.4, Backing Safely

question: Before backing, what should a driver do regarding the path of travel?
choice_a: Ask a passing pedestrian for verbal directions only
choice_b: Rely solely on the back-up camera without leaving the cab
choice_c: Assume the path is clear if no obstacles were seen driving in
choice_d: Get out and walk around the vehicle to check clearance to the sides and overhead
explanation: The manual advises looking at your line of travel before you begin, getting out and walking around the vehicle, and checking clearance to the sides and overhead.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.4, Backing Safely -- Look at Your Path

question: Which gear should a driver use when backing, and why?
choice_a: The same gear used for highway driving
choice_b: Neutral, coasting under gravity
choice_c: The lowest reverse gear, so steering errors can be corrected more easily and the vehicle can stop quickly
choice_d: The highest reverse gear, to complete backing faster
explanation: The manual instructs always backing as slowly as possible using the lowest reverse gear, since that allows easier correction of steering errors and quicker stopping.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.4, Backing Safely -- Back Slowly

question: Why does the manual recommend backing and turning toward the driver's side whenever possible?
choice_a: It allows the driver to see better by looking out the side window
choice_b: It reduces fuel consumption
choice_c: It prevents the parking brake from engaging
choice_d: It is required by federal law in all states
explanation: The manual explains that backing toward the driver's side lets you watch the rear of the vehicle by looking out the side window, while backing toward the right side is dangerous because you can't see as well.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.4, Backing Safely -- Back and Turn Toward the Driver's Side

question: Before backing with a helper, what should the driver and helper agree on?
choice_a: A radio frequency for CB communication only
choice_b: Which mirror the helper will stand behind
choice_c: A set of hand signals, including a signal for 'stop'
choice_d: The exact final resting position to the inch, verbally shouted only
explanation: The manual instructs working out a set of hand signals that both the driver and helper understand before backing, and agreeing on a signal for 'stop.'
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.2.4, Backing Safely -- Use a Helper

question: Which type of manual transmission requires double clutching to change gears?
choice_a: Only vehicles without a clutch pedal
choice_b: All automatic transmissions
choice_c: Vehicles with synchronized manual transmissions
choice_d: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions
explanation: The manual states most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double clutching to change gears, but double clutching is NOT required if equipped with a synchronized manual transmission.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.3.1, Manual Transmissions

topic: Shifting: Recovering from a Missed Gear
question: If a driver remains too long in neutral while double clutching and has difficulty putting the vehicle into the next gear, what should they do?
choice_a: Return to neutral, release the clutch, increase engine speed to match road speed, and try again
choice_b: Apply the parking brake and shift into reverse
choice_c: Turn off the engine and coast into gear
choice_d: Force the gear shift lever until it engages
explanation: The manual advises that if you remain too long in neutral, you should not force the shift, but instead return to neutral, release the clutch, increase engine speed to match road speed, and try again.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.3.1, Manual Transmissions

question: What are the two ways described for knowing when to shift up a manual transmission?
choice_a: Using the fuel gauge or the odometer
choice_b: Using engine speed (rpm) via the tachometer, or using road speed (mph) via the speedometer
choice_c: Counting the number of stop signs passed
choice_d: Listening to the radio volume
explanation: The manual describes two methods: using engine speed (rpm) and watching the tachometer, or using road speed (mph) and watching the speedometer.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.3.1, Knowing When to Shift Up

question: Why should a driver downshift to a lower gear before starting down a hill?
choice_a: To save fuel by coasting in neutral
choice_b: To slow to a speed they can control without using the brakes hard, preventing the brakes from overheating and losing power
choice_c: To reduce noise for nearby residents
choice_d: Because state law requires low gear on all downgrades
explanation: The manual explains that downshifting before a hill lets you control speed without using the brakes hard, since overusing brakes can cause them to overheat and lose braking power.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.3.1, Basic Procedures for Shifting Down

question: What is one benefit of downshifting to the right gear before entering a curve?
choice_a: It eliminates the need to check mirrors in the curve
choice_b: It automatically increases the posted speed limit for the curve
choice_c: It lets you use some power through the curve to help the vehicle stay more stable
choice_d: It disables the vehicle's turn signals
explanation: The manual states that downshifting before a curve lets you use some power through the curve to help the vehicle be more stable while turning, and allows speeding up as soon as you exit the curve.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.3.1, Basic Procedures for Shifting Down -- Before Entering a Curve

question: Why is it important to select a low range on an automatic transmission when going down a grade?
choice_a: It increases fuel consumption for extra power
choice_b: It provides greater engine braking and prevents the transmission from shifting up beyond the selected gear
choice_c: It automatically applies the parking brake
choice_d: It disables the service brakes entirely
explanation: The manual explains that selecting a low range gives greater engine braking, and lower ranges prevent the transmission from shifting up beyond the selected gear (unless the governor rpm is exceeded), making it important to use this braking effect on grades.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.3.3, Automatic Transmissions

question: What are the four basic types of retarders mentioned in the manual?
choice_a: Primary, secondary, tertiary, and emergency
choice_b: Front, rear, side, and center
choice_c: Mechanical, magnetic, pneumatic, and hydraulic
choice_d: Exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric
explanation: The manual lists four basic types of retarders: exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric, which help slow the vehicle and reduce brake wear.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.3.4, Retarders

topic: Retarders: When They Apply Braking Power
question: When turned 'on,' when do retarders apply their braking power to the drive wheels?
choice_a: Whenever the driver lets up on the accelerator pedal all the way
choice_b: Continuously regardless of accelerator position
choice_c: Only when the foot brake is also pressed
choice_d: Only above 60 mph
explanation: The manual states that when turned on, retarders apply their braking power to the drive wheels whenever you let up on the accelerator pedal all the way.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.3.4, Retarders

question: Why should a driver turn off the retarder when the road is wet, icy, or snow covered?
choice_a: Because poor traction can cause the retarder to make the drive wheels skid

question: What is the general rule for following distance at speeds below 40 mph, according to the manual?

choice_b: Two seconds per axle on the vehicle
choice_c: At least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length
choice_d: A fixed 3 seconds regardless of vehicle length
explanation: The manual states the rule that you need at least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length at speeds below 40 mph.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.1, Space Ahead

question: For a 40-foot vehicle traveling below 40 mph, how many seconds of following distance does the manual recommend?

choice_b: 2 seconds
choice_c: 6 seconds
choice_d: 8 seconds
explanation: The manual gives the example that if you are driving a 40-foot vehicle, you should leave 4 seconds between you and the vehicle ahead at speeds below 40 mph.

question: When traveling above 40 mph, what adjustment does the manual say to make to the basic following-distance rule?
choice_a: Subtract 1 second since faster speeds create their own buffer
choice_b: No adjustment is needed above 40 mph
choice_c: Add 1 second for safety
choice_d: Double the base following distance
explanation: The manual states that at speeds greater than 40 mph, you must add 1 second for safety; for example, a 40-foot vehicle would need 5 seconds and a 60-foot vehicle would need 7 seconds.

topic: Space Behind: Staying to the Right
question: If a heavy load is slowing you down going uphill, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Stop on the shoulder until traffic clears
choice_b: Turn on the high beams to warn traffic behind
choice_c: Stay in the right lane if you can, and don't pass another slow vehicle unless you can do so quickly and safely
choice_d: Move to the far left lane to maintain momentum
explanation: The manual advises staying in the right lane if a heavy load is slowing you down going uphill, and not passing another slow vehicle unless you can get around quickly and safely.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.2, Space Behind -- Stay to the Right

question: What does the manual recommend if you find yourself being tailgated?
choice_a: Speed up to put distance between you and the tailgater
choice_b: Turn on your taillights unusually to distract them
choice_c: Avoid quick changes, increase your following distance, and don't speed up
choice_d: Tap your brakes repeatedly to warn the tailgater off
explanation: The manual recommends avoiding quick changes, increasing following distance, not speeding up, and avoiding tricks like flashing brake lights to reduce the chances of a crash when tailgated.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.2, Space Behind -- Dealing with Tailgaters Safely

topic: Space to the Sides: Staying Centered
question: Why is it important to keep a commercial vehicle centered in its lane?
choice_a: It is only a cosmetic preference with no safety benefit
choice_b: It is only relevant on gravel roads
choice_c: It improves fuel economy significantly
choice_d: To keep safe clearance on either side, since wide vehicles have little room to spare
explanation: The manual explains that since commercial vehicles are often wide and take up most of a lane, you need to keep your vehicle centered in the lane to keep safe clearance on either side.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.3, Space to the Sides

topic: Space to the Sides: Traveling Next to Others
question: What are the two dangers of traveling alongside other vehicles, according to the manual?
choice_a: Faster tire wear and brake fade
choice_b: Increased fuel consumption and engine wear
choice_c: Reduced radio reception and mirror glare
choice_d: Another driver may change lanes suddenly into you, and you may be trapped when you need to change lanes
explanation: The manual identifies two dangers of traveling alongside others: another driver may change lanes suddenly and turn into you, and you may be trapped when you need to change lanes.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.3, Space to the Sides -- Traveling Next to Others

question: According to the manual, when is the problem of strong winds affecting lane control often especially bad?
choice_a: Only while parked
choice_b: Only when towing an empty trailer uphill
choice_c: Only on multi-lane interstates
choice_d: Coming out of tunnels
explanation: The manual states that strong winds make it difficult to stay in your lane, and this problem can be especially bad coming out of tunnels; you should avoid driving alongside others if you can.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.3, Space to the Sides -- Strong Winds

question: Why should a driver not simply trust the height posted at a bridge or overpass?
choice_a: Posted heights only apply to passenger cars
choice_b: Bridge heights change daily based on temperature
choice_c: Posted heights are always measured in the wrong units
choice_d: Re-paving or packed snow may have reduced the clearance since the height was posted
explanation: The manual warns not to assume that heights posted at bridges and overpasses are correct, because re-paving or packed snow may have reduced the clearances since the heights were posted.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.4, Space Overhead

topic: Space Overhead: Cargo Van Height Changes
question: Why can a cargo van that cleared a bridge while loaded fail to clear the same bridge later?
choice_a: An empty van is higher than a loaded one, so clearing the bridge loaded does not guarantee clearing it empty
choice_b: Loaded vans are always taller than empty vans
choice_c: Bridges get lower as the day progresses
choice_d: Vans shrink in height when the engine is cold
explanation: The manual explains that the weight of a cargo van changes its height; an empty van is higher than a loaded one, so getting under a bridge while loaded does not mean you can do it empty.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.4, Space Overhead

question: What hazard do drainage channels across roads pose to commercial vehicles, according to the manual?
choice_a: They are only a hazard for motorcycles
choice_b: They can cause the ends of some vehicles to drag, so such depressions should be crossed carefully
choice_c: They cause immediate tire blowouts
choice_d: They increase fuel consumption but pose no mechanical risk
explanation: The manual warns that drainage channels across roads can cause the ends of some vehicles to drag, so such depressions should be crossed carefully.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.5, Space Below

question: If a truck cannot make a right turn without swinging into another lane, what technique does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Swing wide to the left as you start the turn to give more room
choice_b: Turn wide as you complete the turn, keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb
choice_c: Always use the inside lane to complete the turn
choice_d: Back up partway through the turn to reposition
explanation: The manual instructs turning wide as you complete the turn and keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb, which stops other drivers from passing you on the right.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.6, Space for Turns -- Right Turns

topic: Right Turns: Avoiding a Wide Left Start
question: Why does the manual warn against turning wide to the left as you start a right turn?
choice_a: It is illegal in every state to swing left before a right turn
choice_b: A following driver may think you are turning left and try to pass you on the right, causing a crash
choice_c: It causes excessive tire wear on the front axle
choice_d: It confuses the vehicle's turn signal sensor
explanation: The manual warns that if you turn wide to the left as you start the turn, a following driver may think you are turning left and try to pass you on the right, and you may crash into that vehicle as you complete your turn.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.6, Space for Turns -- Right Turns

question: What should a driver do before starting a left turn to avoid hitting another vehicle due to off-tracking?
choice_a: Turn only when the light has been green for over 10 seconds
choice_b: Start the turn as early as possible from the right-hand lane
choice_c: Make sure they have reached the center of the intersection before starting the left turn
choice_d: Accelerate through the intersection before turning
explanation: The manual states that on a left turn, you should make sure you have reached the center of the intersection before starting the left turn, since turning too soon can cause the left side of the vehicle to hit another vehicle because of off-tracking.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.6, Space for Turns -- Left Turns

topic: Left Turns with Two Turning Lanes
question: If there are two left-turn lanes, which one should a large vehicle driver use, and why?
choice_a: The inside lane only, to avoid oncoming traffic
choice_b: The right turn lane, because starting in the inside lane may require swinging right, and drivers on your left can be more readily seen
choice_c: Either lane, since it makes no difference for large vehicles
choice_d: The inside (left) lane, because it is closer to the curb
explanation: The manual instructs always taking the right turn lane when two turning lanes are available, since starting in the inside lane may require swinging right to complete the turn, and drivers on your left can be more readily seen.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.6, Space for Turns -- Left Turns

topic: Space Needed to Cross or Enter Traffic
question: Why do large vehicles need a much larger gap in traffic to enter an intersection than a car would need?
choice_a: Because large vehicles are exempt from yielding right of way
choice_b: Because large vehicles have a shorter wheelbase than cars
choice_c: Because large vehicles have narrower tires
choice_d: Because of slow acceleration and the space large vehicles require
explanation: The manual explains that because of slow acceleration and the space large vehicles require, you may need a much larger gap to enter traffic than you would in a car.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.7.7, Space Needed to Cross or Enter Traffic

question: Before starting across a road, what must a driver make sure of, according to the manual?

choice_d: That the vehicle's headlights are on, even in daylight
explanation: The manual instructs that before you start across a road, you must make sure you can get all the way across before traffic reaches you.
